name: Systems and Control

papers.title: One Neural Operator for Re-planning Low-Thrust Cislunar Transfers after Thrust Outages, at the Original or a Later Arrival
papers.abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.

papers.title: Voltage-Feedback Backoff and Restoration for Priority-Based EV Charging Control
papers.abstract: Uncoordinated residential electric vehicle (EV) charging can cause sustained undervoltage in distribution networks. This paper proposes a centralized voltage-feedback backoff and restoration (VFBR) framework that separates concurrent charging-count control from EV selection. The controller adjusts the allowable charging count using monitored critical-bus voltages, without load forecasts, online power-flow calculations, or optimization. Initial charging suspension relieves undervoltage, followed by group-wise restoration and backoff as voltage conditions permit. A complementary priority score combines charging urgency with voltage sensitivity precomputed offline to balance time-critical requests against their location-dependent voltage impacts. One-week simulations on the unbalanced IEEE 123-bus feeder with 500 EVs show that VFBR reduces the proportion of charging-period bus-time samples below 0.95 p.u. from 15% to less than 1%. Among the evaluated strategies, combined allocation with urgency and sensitivity weights of 0.75 and 0.25 delivers 25% more energy than random allocation and achieves the highest mean departure state of charge and fairness. These results demonstrate that simple voltage-feedback control, coupled with urgency- and sensitivity-based allocation, effectively mitigates undervoltage while improving charging service.

papers.title: Fuel-Efficient Formation Flying via Constrained Extremum Seeking
papers.abstract: This paper presents a model-free autonomous guidance architecture for minimal drag of a trailing aircraft in formation flight. Realizing the fuel savings resulting from such a formation requires learning and tracking a time-varying vortex while avoiding locations where the aircraft experiences an abrupt rolling moment disturbance. A guidance architecture for fuel-efficient safe flight, called Adaptive Plateau-seeking Optimal Guidance with ModulatEd Excitations (APOGEE), is proposed herein. Key features of APOGEE are its ability to modulate the amplitude of the excitation required to learn the unknown objective and constraint functions, to adaptively adjust the learning rates, and to keep the flight safe during the search for the optimal formation. A threshold-gated modulation reduces the amplitude of excitation when the objective function reaches an acceptably large value, thus improving flying qualities and further reducing fuel consumption. Furthermore, a Newton-based learning rule, whose estimate of the inverse of the Hessian is spectrally clamped, adapts the learning rates to the local curvature of the objective function in order to accelerate convergence and lower the chance of overshooting the optimum. Finally, a safety filter having an unknown constraint function is used to prevent a loss of control event prompted by the above mentioned disturbance. The efficacy of APOGEE is demonstrated by using a high-fidelity model of an F-16 jet and an experimentally obtained vortex model. Being model-free, APOGEE does not require modeling the dependence of the unknown functions on the characteristics of the leading aircraft, the flight condition, the crosswind, and the vortex-induced turbulence.

papers.title: MVDC Power Cables for Future Wide-Body All-Electric Aircraft: A Research Journey from System-Level Requirements to Modeling, Design, Fabrication, and Testing
papers.abstract: Future wide-body all-electric aircraft require lightweight electrical distribution systems capable of delivering megawatt-scale propulsion power under demanding thermal and electrical conditions. This article reviews our research program on medium-voltage direct-current (MVDC) power cables, from aircraft-level requirements through modeling, design, fabrication, and low-pressure electrical testing. It connects successive investigations and explains the decisions guiding their development. Aircraft-level power-flow and single-contingency studies establish a +/-5 kV distribution architecture and a 1 kA design objective for the most heavily loaded cable circuits. Coupled electrical, thermal, and airflow models examine multilayer multifunctional electrical insulation, conductor geometry, bipolar pole spacing, duct configuration, and forced convection. Flight-phase studies distinguish higher-current takeoff operation from lower-current operation at reduced cruise pressure. Experiments progress from bonded flat specimens to wrapped cable prototypes, examining fabrication methods, partial discharge, and dielectric breakdown at atmospheric pressure and pressures down to 18.8 kPa. The results highlight the roles of insulation interfaces, wrapping method, cable geometry, and installation conditions in achieving compact designs with improved electrical performance. Together, these studies provide a development framework linking aircraft requirements to manufacturable prototypes. Predicted current-carrying capability is distinguished from measured insulation performance, and the combined electrical, thermal, mechanical, and endurance evaluations needed for aircraft qualification are identified.

papers.title: Optimization of a Hybrid Solar-Biogas-Battery Energy Storage Microgrid: A Case Study
papers.abstract: Low-income regions like eastern Uganda often lack reliable grid power. This paper presents the techno-economic optimization of the Soroti Integrated Renewable Energy Microgrid (SIREM), a hybrid renewable system for grid-access expansion where Soroti District household grid access stands at 16.7\%. The microgrid integrates concentrating solar power (CSP) with thermal storage, biogas combined cycle generation, and lithium iron phosphate battery storage. Using Xendee optimization software with six years of NASA POWER data, the optimal configuration comprises a 37 MW CSP field, 70 MWh molten-salt storage, a 5 MW CSP turbine, a 6 MW biogas CCGT, and a 10 MWh battery system. The design delivers 61.3 GWh annually with a 42.91% IRR, 2-year payback, and levelized cost of electricity of 0.1991 USD/kWh generation (0.3752 USD/kWh load-served), achieving 32.2% total savings versus grid-only supply while exporting 28.8 GWh annually, demonstrating the viability of hybrid renewable microgrids for grid expansion in sub-Saharan Africa.

papers.title: Impact of the Performance of Autonomy and Communication Subsystems on the Level-of-Safety of Partially Autonomous Machine Systems
papers.abstract: The level-of-safety of a partially autonomous machine system depends on two subsystems: the autonomy subsystem that manages the system between human interventions; and the communication subsystem that enables those interventions. These subsystems are typically evaluated independently. We model the level-of-safety analytically as a function of their joint performance. Three parameters characterize the autonomy subsystem: the Mean Time Between Interventions (MTBI); the urgency $\mathcal{U}$ or mean time within which an intervention must be completed to avoid failure; and the complexity $\mathcal{C}$ or mean time to understand, decide on and execute it. Two characterize the communication subsystem: its availability $P_A$ and its latency $\varepsilon$. A dimensionless criticality ratio $\rho=(\mathcal{C}+\varepsilon)/\mathcal{U}$ prescribes the shape of the Pareto tradeoff between the MTBI and $P_A$ at a constant level-of-safety. At $\rho=0.01$, a perfect link lowers the required MTBI by two orders of magnitude. At $\rho=1$, it only halves it. Under exponential timing assumptions the model is in closed form, and compliance with a safety budget can be stated at a chosen assurance level. We illustrate it for remotely piloted aircraft with assumed parameter values and propose a simulation procedure to estimate them.

papers.title: Online Identification Can Replace a Floor-Plan Prior on Unseen Buildings
papers.abstract: The Smart Buildings Challenge asks for one HVAC control policy that runs office buildings and weather it has never seen, from the building's metadata and sensor streams alone. Our controller sees no data from the target building before it runs and is not tuned per building; its few global constants were set on development scenarios. Each zone has a first-order grey-box model that starts from coefficients computed from the floor plan and is updated online by recursive least squares, and a planner and a closed-form mapping turn the models into plant commands. On two sets of buildings and weather that we generated, a validation set and a stress set with real-year weather, it scores 0.145 and 0.159 times the starter kit's PID baseline, and 0.095 times on a holdout built after all versions were fixed and scored once. It improves on every building, also against our two implementations of ASHRAE Guideline 36: per set it scores 0.60 to 0.71 times a basic version and 0.83 to 0.96 times one partly tuned on the public leaderboard, which wins one of 54 scenarios; with a 5 {\deg}C frost target for empty zones on both, the margin over the tuned version shrinks to 1.4% on the stress set, where one of six buildings is 0.2% worse. In an ablation on a reduced-order model, removing both the floor-plan prior and online identification costs 28%, 20% and 42% on the validation, stress and holdout sets, far more than the two effects combined: either source of building-specific information recovers most of what is lost without both. On one office floor in a second simulator, BOPTEST, this does not carry over: with identification on, the two priors give similar results, but the floor-plan prior alone, with constants fitted on the competition's simulator, is the least stable arm. These simulation results motivate testing floor-plan-initialised adaptive control in buildings that have drawings but no operating data.

papers.title: DynaSeek: Large Language Model-Driven Hybrid Dynamic Model Discovery for Grid-Tied Inverters from Limited Measurements
papers.abstract: Discovering the unknown governing equations of grid-tied inverters from limited measurements is essential for the stability analysis of modern inverter-dominated power systems. However, existing identification methods struggle to jointly resolve unmeasured internal control memory and saturation-induced mode transitions from accessible terminal waveforms. To address this challenge, this paper proposes DynaSeek, a large language model (LLM)-driven framework for discovering explicit hybrid differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) of current-limited inverters. The framework integrates physics-constrained symbolic skeleton synthesis with the joint numerical estimation of shared model parameters and record-specific latent initial states across multi-island experience archives. Furthermore, two complementary structural diagnostics evaluating cross-record state closure and cross-window consistency are established to detect structural deficiencies across distinct input histories and transient stages. Guided by diagnostic feedback, DynaSeek directs variable-dimensional latent-state expansion and current-limiting and anti-windup refinement to yield self-contained hybrid DAEs unifying unsaturated regulation, current limiting, and post-fault recovery. Controller-hardware-in-the-loop (CHIL) experiments and closed-loop system-level simulations demonstrate that DynaSeek reduces transient trajectory reconstruction errors by one to two orders of magnitude compared with symbolic and neural baselines while accurately preserving reference critical clearing times, enabling reliable large-signal stability assessment of inverters with inaccessible internal controls.

papers.title: Shared-Harmonic Characterization and Robust Orientation-Selection Certification for Directional Sensing Under Anisotropic Target Motion
papers.abstract: Directional sensors are often oriented using historical target trajectories, while future trajectories remain uncertain at deployment. This letter addresses two post-placement questions: i) when orientation materially affects detection and ii) when a historically selected orientation remains reliable under future target-motion shift. We develop a placement-aware framework for anisotropy-induced detection (AID), showing that orientation sensitivity is governed by harmonic modes shared by the locally visible target-direction distribution and the sensor trajectory-incidence response. The resulting AID measure admits an exact RMS interpretation for the retained-harmonic orientation response. We then introduce a sensor-induced directional discrepancy, derive a conditional bound on future orientation regret, and obtain sufficient certificates for robust orientation selection whenever the future sensor-relevant shift lies within a prescribed discrepancy radius. Using 2025 AIS ship-traffic data near Terrebonne Bay, Louisiana, historical AID is strongly correlated with held-out orientation sensitivity ($r=0.908$). Across four angular-response widths, AID explains orientation-sensitivity variation with $R^2=0.920$, compared with $R^2=0.239$ for target-only anisotropy. At the nominal threshold, 316 of 350 locations are empirically classified as orientation-useful, and all retain gain above the threshold across five held-out windows.

papers.title: Asymptotically Efficient Finite Impulse Response System Identification without Noise Knowledge
papers.abstract: Efficient identification of finite impulse response systems under unknown or heavy-tailed noise remains a challenge in system identification. Classical estimators, including least squares (LS) and robust alternatives like least absolute deviations (LAD), are often sensitive to outliers or statistically inefficient when noise characteristics deviate from their underlying assumptions. To address this, we propose a novel class of adaptive estimators that achieves asymptotic efficiency without requiring prior knowledge of the noise distribution. Our approach leverages kernel density estimation to construct two nonparametric maximum likelihood-type estimators: the estimated maximum likelihood estimator (eMLE) and the estimated profiled MLE (epMLE). These estimators approximate the likelihood using residuals from consistent initial estimates, avoiding parametric assumptions on the noise. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that, under mild regularity conditions, both eMLE and epMLE are consistent, asymptotically normal, and attain the Cram\'er--Rao lower bound, thereby achieving asymptotic efficiency. Additionally, we develop computationally efficient one-step Newton--Raphson algorithms that implement these estimators without sacrificing asymptotic efficiency. Extensive simulations across various noise distributions confirm that the proposed methods outperform classical LS and LAD estimators in both robustness and accuracy, often matching oracle MLE performance.

papers.title: Passivity Shaping over Frequency Bands: A Differentiable Optimization Approach
papers.abstract: The energy transition replaces traditional inertial synchronous machines with power electronic converters, introducing new grid stability challenges. Passivity provides a compositional input-output framework for assessing stability in interconnected grid subsystems, yet tuning controllers for this property over specific frequency ranges - a practical requirement in converter-dominated grids - still relies largely on practitioners' experience, typically based on intuition or trial and error. We address this gap in three steps: (i) we formulate the passivity index over arbitrary frequency bands as the optimal value of a parametric Semidefinite Program (SDP) using the generalized KYP (gKYP) lemma; (ii) we derive analytical sensitivities of this optimal value with respect to controller parameters via the Envelope Theorem; and (iii) we embed these elements in a bilevel optimization scheme that tunes controller parameters to maximize the passivity index. We validate the proposed method on two case studies of increasing complexity: a grid-following converter and a multi-converter microgrid.

papers.title: On the Grouping-based RIS-aided Multi-user Networks: A Graph Theoretic Approach
papers.abstract: In this letter, we propose a graph theoretic framework for grouping-based reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-aided multi-user wireless networks. By considering both the ideal as well as the practical RIS-based phase shift models, the aspect of the RIS-user association is formulated as a graph matching problem. Thereafter, we derive conditions, which on satisfying, guarantee that the ideal RIS-based optimal RIS-user association remains uniquely optimal even in the practical RIS-based scenario. Finally, extensive Monte Carlo simulations validate the importance of the proposed framework.

papers.title: MIMOS: A Toolbox for Multivariable Modal Identification
papers.abstract: Accurate and physically interpretable models are essential for the analysis and control of complex multivariable systems. This paper presents the Multivariable Identification of Modal Optical and mechatronic Systems (MIMOS) toolbox, an open-source MATLAB toolbox for identifying physical modal models from measured multivariable frequency response functions. The two-stage approach first estimates an additive input-output model from measured frequency responses and subsequently recovers the physical modal structure through information-weighted projection. MIMOS implements this approach in a practical and scalable workflow combining frequency response preprocessing, interactive modal initialization and refinement, and support for proportional and general viscous damping. Experimental results on a publicly available $6\times8$ vibration isolation benchmark and a $7\times17$ prototype wafer stage demonstrate the capability of MIMOS to effectively handle identification problems involving thousands of parameters and estimate accurate, minimal-order physical modal models.

papers.title: Passive Fault-Tolerant Antenna Stabilisation for Ship-to-Shore Communication
papers.abstract: Directional ship-to-shore radio links require continuous antenna alignment with the shore station, while vessel heave induces variations in antenna height above the sea surface, thereby altering the multipath interference governing the received power. In conventional stabilised gimbals, attitude compensation is provided, whereas fault tolerance is rarely considered. To address these limitations, a passive fault-tolerant control scheme is proposed, whereby the antenna is mounted on a ship-mounted six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, enabling simultaneous regulation alignment and antenna height. Through feedback linearisation, the manipulator dynamics are decoupled into perturbed integrators, each controlled by a multi-barrier adaptive super-twisting sliding-mode controller. The nested barriers are associated with the performance regions of fault-tolerant control, such that inter-sample barrier crossings under discrete-time implementation lead to graceful performance degradation rather than loss of confinement. Under simulated conditions, superior pointing and heave accuracy is achieved compared with single-barrier designs, for which either precision or confinement is compromised.

papers.title: Travelling-Wave-Based Protection of DC Hubs in Bipolar HVDC Grids
papers.abstract: This paper presents a stationary wavelet transform (SWT)-based method for DC fault detection and classification in a three-terminal bipolar modular multilevel converter (MMC)-based HVDC system with a dedicated metallic return (DMR). The system incorporates DC switching stations (DCSSs) with interconnected DC circuit breakers (DCCBs). The method uses line-mode voltage wavelet detail energy for fault detection and wavelet detail energy derived from pole voltages and DMR current for fault classification, distinguishing pole-to-pole, pole-to-ground, and pole-to-DMR faults. Its performance is evaluated using a real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) platform integrating an real-time digital simulator (RTDS) with embedded processing hardware. Busbar and cable faults with varying fault types, resistances, and locations are investigated. The results demonstrate the feasibility of real-time implementation and characterize the effects of fault location and travelling-wave propagation on transient energy and protection response time. The effectiveness of pole-voltage and DMR-current detail energy features in distinguishing fault types is also evaluated.

papers.title: Decentralized Control Barrier Function Filters for Frequency Containment With Inverters
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the design of safety filters for grid-following (GFL) inverters in power transmission systems. The goal of the filters is to constrain frequency nadir and zenith following generation-demand imbalances, by supplementing primary frequency control. Using a reduced electromechanical model and control barrier functions (CBFs), we define an ideal filter through a convex quadratic program (QP). The ideal QP filter renders the set of admissible frequencies forward invariant; however, its direct implementation is impractical, as it requires centralized implementation and model-based computation. We then use a dual proximal formulation and a two-time-scale implementation to obtain decentralized dynamic filters that can be implemented at each inverter and use only local frequency and rate-of-change-of-frequency estimates. To assess the performance and the ability to regulate frequency, we derive bounds on the distance between state trajectories under the dynamic and ideal CBF filters. The bounds quantify the effects of the filter time constant, initialization, load variation, and frequency estimation errors, and provide estimates of possible frequency-limit violations. We validate the proposed method on the IEEE 39-bus system using a high-fidelity electromagnetic-transient (EMT) model.

papers.title: Grey-Box Experimental Identification of Reduced-Order Models for Grid-Forming Converters
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a grey-box system identification for identifying and validating reduced-order models (ROMs) of grid-forming (GFM) converters. Three reduced-order modeling techniques are compared within a common identification procedure: singular perturbation with frequency cutoff and participation factors (SP-PF), singular perturbation with energy residuals (SP-Energy), and balanced truncation (BT). Testing is on experimental data with real-life components. Results show that BT achieves the highest time-domain fit, followed by SP-Energy and SP-PF; SP-Energy better preserves key properties of the identified full-order model; BT places the dominant mode closest to the stability boundary and exhibits the highest sensitivity to parameter variations; SP-Energy outperforms SP-PF in both fit quality and consistency of modal preservation. Findings suggest that the model with the best time-domain fit does not always provide the most reliable representation of the modal properties for small-signal stability, with SP-Energy offering the best compromise between accuracy, physical interpretability, and modal preservation for the considered case study.

papers.title: Gaussian Processes for Optimal Space-Filling Input Design
papers.abstract: The quality of a model resulting from (black-box) system identification is highly dependent on the quality of the data that is used during the identification procedure. As nonlinear system identification is sensitive to modeling and extrapolation errors, having experiments that explore the considered operation range of interest are of high importance. The Gaussian-Process based space-filling input design strategy introduces an experiment design technique that aims to achieve a space-filling distribution within the argument space of a (nonlinear) approximator used for modeling the true system. Experiments carried out on simulation examples show that models trained with space-filling signals generalize better over the region of interest compared to models obtained from non-space-filling experiments. Moreover, the method is connected to the optimality theory of experiment design (V- and D-optimal design), allowing the experimenter to tailor the designed space-filling signal to maximize its information content with respect to the experiment objective.

papers.title: Azimuth Pointing and Momentum Management for a Lightweight High-Altitude Balloon Payload
papers.abstract: The ALTAIR (Airborne Laser for Telescopic Atmospheric Interference Reduction) project provides photometric calibration for ground-based telescopes by flying an integrating sphere as an artificial star-like calibration source on a high-altitude balloon. Because the angular distribution of light from the exit port of the sphere is approximately Lambertian, the payload must keep its azimuth within $\pm8^\circ$ of the telescope line of sight. This condition bounds the fractional difference in light intensity from that along the exit-port normal to below 1%. The bound must be held for at least 30 s at a time. This paper presents a pointing architecture that combines passive stabilization, onboard attitude determination, and active azimuth control using a momentum wheel, with active desaturation through a second motor at the flight-train pivot. Carbon-fiber inertial booms reduce off-axis pendulating motion sufficiently for azimuth control to be treated independently. Attitude is determined by onboard fusion of rate gyro, accelerometer, magnetometer, and dual-antenna GNSS carrier-phase measurements. A high-fidelity simulation of the payload, including motor dynamics and limits, sensor noise, and wind disturbances generated from flight data, is used to size actuators and tune the control loops. The payload avionics, flight software, power management, controls, and real-time ground telemetry systems are developed in-house. The system is evaluated through ground testing, simulation, and two flights. With the momentum wheel alone, 53 intervals of 30 s pointing within $\pm8^\circ$ of the target azimuth are recorded during ascent, with a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of $3.7^\circ$, and the longest uninterrupted window lasts 7 min 55 s with $5^\circ$ of pointing RMSE. Simulation results suggest significant performance improvements from adding a pivot motor for momentum management.

papers.title: Adaptive Control Barrier Functions for Nonlinear Singularly Perturbed Systems
papers.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) have emerged as a flexible and efficient approach for enforcing dynamic safety constraints. In this paper, we consider a class of uncertain nonlinear systems with singular perturbations and develop an adaptive CBF framework for such systems to enforce safety constraints on both the slow and fast subsystems in the overall singularly perturbed nonlinear system with uncertain parameters. We first develop a robustness property showing that if an adaptive controller for the slow subsystem satisfies the slow CBF condition with an appropriate safety margin, then for sufficiently small values of the singular perturbation parameter $\varepsilon$, the slow subsystem remains within an $O(\varepsilon)$-neighborhood of its safe set. We then consider the more general case of safety constraints on both the fast and slow subsystems and provide conditions under which joint slow-fast safety is achieved despite the parametric uncertainties. The reduced-order slow model and the slow and fast CBF conditions are evaluated using an online parameter estimate and the parameter mismatch between the estimated and true reduced-order models is addressed via a state-dependent robustness margin in the CBF inequalities. To illustrate the proposed framework, we present simulation studies for two systems with parametric uncertainties: a synthetic two-time-scale fourth-order example system and a unicycle with a fast turn-rate actuator and an obstacle avoidance safety constraint.

papers.title: Real Package, Wrong Controller: Static Auditing of Vendor--Protocol Mismatches in LLM-Generated PLC Code
papers.abstract: Language models can generate Python that drives industrial protocols on programmable logic controllers, yet existing code-grounding checks ask whether an imported package or symbol exists rather than whether it suits the declared industrial target. We define \emph{metadata-conditioned, import-level vendor--protocol incompatibility} and build \textsc{Proteus-OT}, a label-free static verifier over a version-pinned graph of documented bindings. Across 883 generated scripts, 180 carry an import-level mismatch against the declared target (20.4\%); restricting to single-vendor targets gives 16.3\%, and additionally requiring the offending library to reach a protocol communication call gives 14.2\%, which we read as conditional on the corpus metadata rather than on verified intent. None of the 28 adjudicable human control files carries one, a sample too small to estimate a prevalence. Within the balanced subset, 96.6\% of mismatching scripts import packages and call methods that exist, so an existence baseline does not represent them, and every positive ships with an inspectable witness. We also audit machine-versus-human classification on the same corpus, where character $n$-grams reach macro-F1 1.000 under task, model and vendor-disjoint partitions and survive comment removal, an AST round trip and identifier anonymisation. The trailing newline present in 95.2\% of human files and in none of the generated ones separates the classes on its own. Vendor--protocol consistency is a useful static audit target, whereas provenance classification on repository-labelled corpora is not authorship detection.

papers.title: Discovering Explicit Magnetic Core-Loss Equations via Symbolic Sparse Identification
papers.abstract: Compact core loss equations are essential tools in magnetic component design, but existing approaches trade accuracy against interpretability. Empirical models such as the Steinmetz Equation (SE) yield compact expressions of limited accuracy, while machine learning methods achieve high accuracy as black-box predictors. This paper bridges the gap with a Symbolic Sparse Identification (SSI) framework, which casts core loss modeling as a data-driven symbolic regression problem and recovers unknown equations directly from measured data, without presuming a functional form. First, a comprehensively expanded library of symbolic candidate terms far richer than the SE is constructed. Second, the governing terms are isolated from this library by sparse regression. Third, the coefficients of the retained terms are refined with an AdamW optimizer to maximize accuracy and form an analytical equation. Experiments on Fair-Rite 78, 79, and 95 yield test mean absolute percentage errors of 1.89%, 1.01%, and 1.56%, respectively, with only 10, 10, and 7 active terms. Comparisons with empirical, numerical, and symbolic models quantify the resulting balance of accuracy and compactness. SSI thus provides an explicit and physically guided approach for high-frequency magnetic characterization and design.

papers.title: Model Predictive Control of a Multirotor UAV with a Cable-Suspended Payload: A Comparison of Shifted and Transformer-Based Warm Starts
papers.abstract: This study investigates model predictive control (MPC) of a multirotor drone (unmanned aerial vehicle, UAV) carrying a cable-suspended payload, comparing conventional shifted initialization with Transformer-based warm starting of a sequential convex programming (SCP) optimizer. The controller uses a coupled mechanical model with an elastic cable and a double-pendulum representation of the suspended load. Its formulation includes move-blocked control inputs, finite-difference sensitivities, constrained quadratic subproblems, and input-feasibility projection. A Transformer trained on expert SCP solutions predicts an initial control sequence, which is subsequently refined by the same optimizer used for the conventional methods. Numerical experiments compare zero, shifted, and Transformer initialization under identical controller settings. For independently solved MPC problems, Transformer initialization reduces computation time relative to zero initialization. In sequential closed-loop simulations, however, shifting the preceding optimized control sequence provides the lowest computation time, while all three methods produce similar tracking behavior. These findings emphasize the importance of comparing learned warm starts with conventional initialization methods that reuse previous MPC solutions. The measured optimization times exceed the control sampling period; consequently, real-time implementation is not demonstrated. Keywords: Model predictive control; sequential convex programming; Transformer; warm start; cable-suspended payload; multirotor drone.

papers.title: The Phases of Hierarchy
papers.abstract: We develop a dynamical phase theory of hierarchy, in which depth decides whether a population of size $N$ that revises its own environment can correct it without overcorrecting. The statistics that let a large majority detect a small bias - the basis of the Condorcet jury theorem - also make its response grow as $\sqrt{N}$. Fed back into the environment it is judging, this sharpening destabilises the matched state through a flip bifurcation at a critical loop gain, which we obtain analytically for a class of models we term adaptive normal forms. We show that this instability can be attenuated by hierarchical layering, requiring a depth scaling logarithmically with $N$. This recovers known logarithmic bounds in organisational economics directly from dynamic stability conditions. Hierarchical depth carries its own costs however, and by analysing the signal chain transmission up the hierarchy we show that beyond a finite depth no correction reaches the top before its deadline, and that below it the cost of arrival grows exponentially with depth. A hierarchy that is too flat therefore oscillates and one that is too deep cannot be steered in time, leaving a bounded window of depth between an unstable flat phase and a frozen inertial phase. We further show that these results can be generalised by treating each layer as a real-space renormalisation step, classifying aggregation rules by how they transmit bias. This establishes a connection between these dynamic results to attention in Transformers, where a residual update is diffusion on the token graph and depth plays the role of scale. Finally we show these phase boundaries are observable in finite sampling, and propose measurements which may characterise the proposed phases in real adaptive systems.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Learning for Multiplayer Differential Games
papers.abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.

papers.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
papers.abstract: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.

papers.title: A general-purpose safe manipulator planning framework for diverse environments without retraining
papers.abstract: Nowadays, robots need to be retrained whenever their operating environment changes, and this prohibitive training cost keeps them far from daily use. The community is calling for innovations that bestow on a robot the ability to safely grasp different objects under different conditions without excessive training data and computing power. In response to this call, we present a general-purpose manipulator mission-planning framework, allowing a robot to safely perform manipulation tasks, such as grasping objects that fit in its gripper, across different operating environments without retraining its controllers. The framework rests on two innovations: a finite-state abstracted model, bisimilar to the original system dynamics, that describes accessibility of the space in front of the robot under its given arm and gripper, and a block-conservative specification generation method that turns each manipulation task under any specific operational environment into specifications about state accessibility of the abstracted model. A task proven feasible and safe on the abstracted model is guaranteed to be safe and achievable by the robot. Real-world case studies conducted on a Unitree G1 U1 humanoid show that manipulation tasks commonly encountered in daily life, such as grasping an object, pressing an elevator button or picking up a berry, can be handled within this framework, where an abstracted model of the G1 U1 robot is built only once to avoid costly model reconstructions, and different tasks are simply captured by specific block-conservative specifications, achievable by a generic mission planner with vision-based feedback control.

papers.title: Robust Adaptive Channel Estimation for RIS-Assisted mmWave Massive MIMO via a Stochastic Shannon Entropy Criterion
papers.abstract: Accurate channel estimation in reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems remains challenging due to the passive nature of the RIS, the high dimensionality of the cascaded channel, and the presence of non-Gaussian impulsive disturbances. This paper proposes a robust sparsity-aware adaptive estimator, termed reweighted zero-attracting stochastic Shannon entropy (RZA-SSE), for angular-domain channel estimation. The algorithm combines a double-window kernel-based Shannon entropy criterion with a norm-normalized \(\ell_1\) penalty. Both the data-driven term and the nonsmooth penalty are differentiated using exact Wirtinger calculus. An exact weight-error recursion and a mean-square energy relation are derived. Local stability is analyzed via a joint coefficient--penalty state representation, and an approximate steady-state mean-square deviation (MSD) expression is obtained. Extensive simulations under Gaussian-mixture impulsive noise demonstrate that ZA-SSE consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art benchmarks in steady-state MSD.

papers.title: Ensuring Deployment-Time Safety of Neural Network Controlled Systems via Localized Certificate Repair
papers.abstract: Barrier certificates provide formal safety guarantees for neural network controlled systems by ensuring that system trajectories avoid unsafe regions over time. However, after deployment, previously unseen obstacles or constraint changes may introduce new unsafe regions, invalidating the original certificate and potentially leading to unsafe behavior. We address this setting with adaptive piecewise barrier certificates, which preserve the original certificate and policy in unchanged regions while introducing localized updates around newly emerged unsafe regions. The central question is how to perform such updates efficiently during system execution without retraining from scratch. Our key idea is to cast deployment-time adaptation as a localized certificate repair problem and reduce it to an optimization task that leverages the learned structure of previous barrier certificates, enabling fast updates without global retraining. We further design a staged repair framework that progressively transitions from localized repair to joint policy-certificate updates and, when necessary, localized retraining. Empirical results on four benchmarks with five new obstacles show that our method succeeds in all cases and completes within tens of seconds on average, whereas retraining from scratch fails in most cases. On instances where retraining succeeds, our method is 17.3$\times$ faster on average. It incurs only 16.2% performance degradation relative to the original policy.

papers.title: A Robust Optimization Framework for Energy System Capacity Expansion under Line Outage Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Capacity expansion models are widely used in climate and energy policy analysis to find optimal investments in generation, storage, and transmission. As the share of renewable generation grows, these models rely more on transmission lines to balance supply and demand across regions. Transmission lines, however, can fail due to aging, extreme weather, or accidents. Models that represent outages as time-dependent events come mainly from electrical engineering and are applied to small-scale systems, as they quickly become computationally intractable for inter-regional capacity expansion. We develop a capacity expansion model in which the risk of line failures shapes the investments in all parts of the system. We formulate it as a two-stage, scenario-based robust optimization problem that samples time-varying outage scenarios from a Markov model and hedges the investments against the most severe ones. To solve the model, we propose a memory-augmented Benders decomposition algorithm combined with Monte Carlo simulation that can handle thousands of scenarios. The selected plan is then evaluated with an out-of-sample simulation to bound the Value-at-Risk (VaR) of its system cost. In a 25-node case study of Germany and its neighboring countries, the gap between the lower bound and the simulated VaR bound is below 1%. We compare the robust plans with a deterministic plan, which assumes all lines are always available, and with a reserve-margin heuristic, which requires local firm capacity to be above peak demand. Like the heuristic, the robust plans nearly eliminate loss of load in 1000 simulated outage scenarios. Their mean system cost is within 0.2% of the deterministic plan and about 4.5% below the heuristic. Instead of adding more generation capacity, the robust approach mainly changes the type and location of capacity, for example, by spreading storage across the network.

papers.title: SOC-Net: Second-Order-Cone-Constrained Neural Networks
papers.abstract: In many applications, neural networks must learn input-output maps that respect prior knowledge such as physical laws, safety requirements, and operating limits. These requirements constrain which outputs are admissible for a given input and often admit second-order cone (SOC) representations, including norm bounds and robust linear inequalities. Examples in control include friction cones, thrust bounds, and input-robust control barrier function (CBF) conditions. However, existing approaches to enforcing general input-dependent SOC constraints require a conic solver, an iterative scheme whose feasibility depends on convergence, or an interior feasible point for each input. We propose SOC-Net, a neural network architecture that enforces input-dependent SOC constraints by construction for every input, even outside the training distribution. SOC-Net projects an affine lifting of the backbone output onto the reachable slice of a fixed product of Lorentz cones and maps the correction back to the output space. For separable constraints, this projection splits into one projection per cone, and each is available in closed form or reduces to a single scalar equation, regardless of the cone dimension. We prove that SOC-Net retains the expressive power of the backbone network under regularity conditions and accommodates end-to-end training by standard backpropagation with an explicit Jacobian. Experiments on contact force allocation with friction constraints and 3-D obstacle avoidance with an input-robust CBF demonstrate that SOC-Net satisfies the constraints at every evaluated input, with lower evaluation latency than the tested solver-based and iterative baselines.

papers.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

papers.title: Recoverability policy editing for closed-loop safety in autonomous driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.

papers.title: Decision-Focused Learning for Multistage Stochastic Programs, with Application to Power Network Repair Scheduling
papers.abstract: Multistage stochastic programs (MSPs) with discrete decisions are hard to solve due to the curse of dimensionality, non-convex value functions, and scenario trees that grow exponentially with the horizon. We develop a decision-focused learning (DFL) framework for MSPs in which a neural network predicts scores for the part of the decision that drives the state transition. Under structural conditions that make this sub-decision enter the stage objective linearly, the network is trained on labels from offline single-scenario problems, using the Fenchel-Young loss with perturbed optimizers, which need only an optimization oracle. We apply the framework to repair scheduling in power networks under stochastic, time-varying component failures, with and without a per-stage repair budget. On a synthetic 5-bus network and on the IEEE 14-bus network at two repair-cost scales, the learned and baseline policies are compared on common evaluation paths. Without the budget, DFL is the cheapest policy on the 5-bus network; on the 14-bus network it does not outperform a near-sighted model-predictive control (MPC) baseline, but it beats repairing every failed component at the higher scale. Under a binding budget, DFL is the cheapest policy evaluated on both networks and at both scales, 14% to 23% below the next-best policy. On the 5-bus network, the mean cost of DFL is 1.7% (without the budget) and 1.8% (with it) above the exact optimum computed by dynamic programming. Within days of computation, sample average approximation yields costlier policies than DFL and the repair-everything heuristic, and stochastic dual dynamic integer programming remains far from convergence. DFL computes its decisions about as fast as the trivial heuristics and orders of magnitude faster than MPC. Since these conditions are not specific to power networks, the framework extends to other MSPs that share this structure.

papers.title: AFM metrology for 3D high aspect ratio semiconductor structures
papers.abstract: Transistors have long been the foundation of the semiconductor industry, with continuous architectural innovations enabling the scaling of integrated circuits while maintaining high performance. Advancements in deposition and lithographic techniques have further expanded design possibilities, while increasing structural complexity demands stricter process control. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) offers a rapid and reliable metrology solution, providing high-resolution measurements and robust statistical analysis of critical parameters. In this work, we present clearly resolved individual profiles of lines and spaces in high aspect ratio (HAR) gate all around FET (GAAFET)-type structures on both the nanosheet (NS) region and in the isolation region between the nanosheets and we present a comprehensive statistical evaluation of their critical dimensions.

papers.title: $\mu$MPC: Microsecond-Scale Nonlinear and World Model Control from Edge to GPU via Koopman-Linearized Precompilation
papers.abstract: We present $\mu$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $\mu$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $\mu$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23\mu$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.

papers.title: Adaptive Reliability Reserves for Residential Battery Fleets
papers.abstract: In a Houston 2024 replay, replacing a fixed 20 percent battery reserve with a county-risk threshold raises observed five-hour backup coverage from 75.0 percent to 86.5 percent and adds USD 10.2 in modeled annualized margin per home (paired 95 percent interval: USD +1.7 to USD +21.7). The paired coverage-gain interval includes zero. This is a conditional simulation result, not measured company reliability. Residential batteries face this tradeoff because market discharge consumes energy also needed for household outages. We release HomeFleet-ERCOT, combining observed prices and county outages with identified simulated homes and causal controller inputs. We compare independent-home optimization with 21 proximal policy optimization (PPO) training runs; ten promise-cost candidates span 31.1 percent-96.3 percent backup coverage. Of these, 10 have lower modeled margin than fixed 20 percent, and 3 also have lower coverage. Chronological, geographic, fleet, and storm tests examine transfer. An alert charging override has a conditional energy-and-power sufficiency guarantee, but only 19.5 percent of 41 county mass-outage episodes provide enough continuous warning for every battery preset. Synthetic tests include short, missed, and false warnings, load uplift, capacity loss, and dropout. A static AC audit retains existing feeder violations; aging comparisons expose model sensitivity. The released benchmark, controllers, and checkpoints provide a reproducible basis for comparing these tradeoffs. This work supports the design of residential battery programs that assess market value and household backup service together.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.
